item.research_question: Can a combination of machine learning, phenomenological rules, and CALPHAD modeling be used to predict the yield strength of refractory high-entropy alloys in the Al-Cr-Nb-Ti-V-Zr system?
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc melting, with a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, and homogenization annealing at 1200 °C for 10 h
item.test_conditions: Compression tests at 20 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C, with an initial strain rate of 10−4 s−1
key_findings: The surrogate model based on a support-vector machine algorithm showed good accuracy at 20 °C and 600 °C, with a prediction error of less than 20% for all alloys except one.
At 800 °C, the error of prediction was worse than 20% for only two model alloys.
The content of aluminum, chromium, and zirconium have the greatest influence on the specific yield strength.
The effect of vanadium and titanium is lower; an addition of niobium has a negative effect on specific yield strength.
One of the predicted alloys (A5: Al13Cr12Nb20Ti20V35) possesses an excellent combination of strength and ductility in the interval 20–800 °C.
item.mechanism: The authors suggest that the relatively low prediction accuracy at 800 °C can be associated with the proximity of this temperature to the transition point between the athermal plateau and the strong temperature dependence in bcc alloys.
item.limitations: The authors note that the proposed approach requires further improvement through the involvement of additional models and computing methods.
item.future_work: Prospective work should focus on (i) an improvement of the prediction accuracy, especially at high temperatures and (ii) an expansion of the predicted characteristics (e.g., ductility, oxidation resistance, etc.).
quotes: The use of a combination of CALPHAD and phenomenological rules does not result in an accurate prediction of the phase composition of the alloys;
The surrogate model based on a support-vector machine algorithm for the prediction of the yield strength showed good accuracy at 20 °C and 600 °C

Relatively low prediction accuracy at 800 °C can be associated with the proximity of this temperature to the transition point between the athermal plateau and the strong temperature dependence in bcc alloys
